section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department correspondence, diplomatic despatches, and analytical memoranda from May 1935 through early 1936 concerning political developments, economic trends, and civil-military relations in Japan. The documents examine the ongoing preeminence of the military under Foreign Minister Koki Hirota, the creation by imperial ordinance of the Cabinet Deliberative Council and Cabinet Investigation Bureau, and mounting industrial nationalism highlighted by army resistance to the expansion of foreign automotive plants such as the Ford Motor Company. Additional files cover factional purges within the Japanese army following the removal of General Jinsaburo Masaki and the assassination of Major General Nagata, the reduction of sentences for civilian plotters of the May 15 Incident under the Naval Criminal Code, court personnel transitions including Count Makino's resignation, and strategic Japanese maneuvers toward North China and Inner Mongolia.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew analyzes the foreign policy of Foreign Minister Hirota, the enduring influence of the military, and Hirota's political standing and connections to the Kokuryu Kai.
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of an Embassy despatch evaluates the domestic forces shaping Japanese foreign policy under Foreign Minister Koki Hirota. Grew emphasizes that despite a less bellicose surface tone, the military retains its guiding dominance and merely supports Hirota's non-military tactics because they offer an economical method to secure the Empire's objectives. Hirota's political strength is shown to rest heavily upon his longstanding affiliation with the patriotic Kokuryu Kai (Black Dragon Society), which he leverages to restrain right-wing extremism while obtaining powerful civilian backing. The Ambassador advises that American policy should not anticipate democratic developments in Japan, as military leaders and committed nationalists remain firmly in control.
subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Policy, the Influence of the Military, and Hirota's Relations with Nationalist Societies

subfiles.about: A document file note cross-referencing a letter from Ambassador Bingham in London regarding the Japanese Ambassador's views on military control in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference note records a letter dated April 29, 1935, from Ambassador Robert W. Bingham in Great Britain, filed under 841.002/139. The letter summarizes a conversation with the Japanese Ambassador to Great Britain concerning Japan's internal situation. The Japanese Ambassador expressed regret regarding recent actions resulting from military dominance and voiced hope that the situation could be gradually overcome.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Conversation with the Japanese Ambassador to Great Britain

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing and analyzing Tokyo despatch No. 1332 regarding the establishment of two new cabinet advisory bodies.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reviews Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 1332 reporting the establishment by Imperial Ordinances of the Cabinet Deliberative Council (Naikaku Shingi Kai) and the Cabinet Investigation Bureau (Naikaku Chosa Kyoku). Turner notes that the Deliberative Council consists of cabinet-caliber politicians, peers, and business leaders without military representation, while the Investigation Bureau, headed by Shigeru Yoshida, includes expert civil servants and lower-ranking army and navy officers. The memorandum explains that public dissatisfaction with parliamentary government and the absence of the Genro spurred the creation of these coordinating organs. It concludes that the military chose to participate only in technical planning to avoid being bound by the political council's decisions.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1332 Regarding the Cabinet Deliberative Council and Cabinet Investigation Bureau

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on the creation, structure, membership, and political implications of the Cabinet Deliberative Body and Cabinet Investigation Bureau.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1332 provides an extensive analysis of Imperial Ordinances Nos. 118 and 119 of May 10, 1935, which created two new advisory bodies subordinate to the Japanese Cabinet. The Cabinet Deliberative Body (Naikaku Shingi Kai), presided over by Premier Okada with Finance Minister Takahashi as vice president, serves as a high-level consultative board composed of prominent peers, business magnates, and party politicians, entirely excluding military officers. In contrast, the Cabinet Investigation Bureau (Naikaku Chosa Kyoku), directed by former Chief Cabinet Secretary Shigeru Yoshida, functions as a research and planning organ staffed by ministerial specialists and mid-ranking army and navy officers. Grew observes that these bodies emerge from deep-seated dissatisfaction with party politics and a perceived need for state-led national coordination, though their ultimate constitutional status and practical effectiveness remain uncertain.
subfiles.title: Cabinet Deliberative Body and Cabinet Investigation Bureau

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing difficulties encountered by the Ford Motor Company in acquiring land to expand its Yokohama factory.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum digests Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 1345 regarding a meeting between Embassy Counselor Edwin L. Neville and Benjamin Kopf, manager of Ford's Yokohama plant. Kopf explained that efforts to purchase expansion land from Yokohama City and private owners were abruptly broken off due to opposition from Japanese army authorities. Kopf decided to postpone the purchase until nationalist sentiment subsided, observing that domestic vehicle manufacturers offered negligible competition because of rigid military specifications.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1345 Regarding Ford Motor Company Land Purchase in Yokohama

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits a memorandum of conversation with the manager of the Ford plant in Yokohama concerning military obstruction of plant expansion.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1345 reports on the rising nationalist and exclusionary tendencies in Japanese industry, enclosing a memorandum of conversation between Embassy Counselor Edwin L. Neville and Benjamin Kopf, manager of the Ford Motor Company in Yokohama. Kopf recounted that after the City of Yokohama refused to sell land for factory expansion, the Asano interests also terminated negotiations for a tract at Tsurumi after being warned by the War Department. Neville advised patience rather than formal diplomatic intervention or legal action, explaining that cyclical waves of anti-foreign nationalism were historically common in Japan. Kopf agreed to bide his time, noting that if necessary, the company could expand vertically on its existing property.
subfiles.title: Nationalist Tendencies in Japanese Industry

subfiles.about: A document file note cross-referencing Tokyo Telegram No. 143 regarding Prime Minister Okada's control over military policy in China.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Tokyo Embassy Telegram No. 143, dated June 29, 1935, filed under 793.94/7128. The telegram reports on the political situation in Japan, emphasizing Prime Minister Keisuke Okada's firm control over events in China and his exceptionally strong standing among the empire's leading statesmen.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Political Situation in Japan and Attitude of Prime Minister Okada

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports confidential assurances that Prime Minister Okada is fully in control of China policy and committed to peaceful settlements.
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 143 conveys confidential information from a reliable source stating that Prime Minister Keisuke Okada considers himself fully in control of Japanese operations in China and is resolved to prevent major military actions in favor of peaceful adjustments. The informant described Okada as holding a stronger position than any recent premier, pointing out that he is the sole moderate survivor of the London Naval Conference controversy still in high active office. Okada anticipated possible localized incidents instigated by overzealous younger officers, but expressed confidence that, backed by the imperial court, he could prevent them from developing into wider crises.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 143 from Tokyo Regarding Prime Minister Okada's Policy on China

subfiles.about: Chargé Neville analyzes the dismissal of General Jinsaburo Masaki as Inspector General of Military Education and its implications for army discipline.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1414 provides an extensive analysis of the removal of General Jinsaburo Masaki from his post as Inspector General of Military Education following a sharp dispute with Minister of War Senjuro Hayashi over personnel promotions. Hayashi, seeking to restore discipline and end political clique activities that emerged during the Manchurian crisis, forced Masaki out with imperial sanction and initiated extensive reassignments affecting over 3,000 officers. The despatch reviews the leadership changes in the military since the Mukden Incident of 1931, noting that Masaki had previously utilized the gendarmerie under General Hata to monitor rivals. Neville emphasizes that Masaki's replacement by the moderate General Jotaro Watanabe represents an internal army movement to curb insubordination, corroborating Foreign Minister Hirota's view that extremist machinations within the military would temporarily decline.
subfiles.title: Removal of General Masaki

subfiles.about: Chargé Neville reports on Ford's acquisition of land following General Masaki's removal and discusses planned Japanese automotive licensing legislation.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1422 reports on the successful resolution of the Ford Motor Company's land purchase difficulties in Yokohama, enclosing correspondence with manager Benjamin Kopf and a memorandum of conversation with Saburo Kurusu, Chief of the Foreign Office Commercial Bureau. Following informal discussions and advice from Neville to consider legal action against the Asano interests, military objections abruptly vanished and Ford secured title to the property on July 30, coinciding with the personnel shakeup that ousted General Masaki. The despatch also reveals that the War Department is promoting legislation to establish a licensing system for the automobile industry aimed at fostering domestic manufacturing. Neville notes that this development was promptly brought to the attention of both Ford and General Motors executives.
subfiles.title: Nationalist Tendencies in Japanese Industry: Settlement of Ford Land Purchase

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum discussing Tokyo despatch No. 1436 and two articles by H. G. Woodhead analyzing Japan's expansionist motivations.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reviews Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 1436, which transmitted two articles from Oriental Affairs authored by British journalist H. G. Woodhead. The articles examine Japanese actions on the Asiatic continent from Japan's perspective, arguing that Western powers must grant Japan economic access to foreign markets if they wish to halt territorial expansion. Turner observes that Woodhead's analysis aligns closely with Ambassador Grew's previous despatches and draws attention to the views of British observers cited in the covering report.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1436 Regarding Urge Toward Expansion in Japan

subfiles.about: Chargé Neville transmits articles by H. G. Woodhead and analyzes the economic pressures and international trade barriers driving Japanese expansion.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1436 transmits clippings from the Japan Advertiser reprinting a two-part essay from Oriental Affairs, attributed to British journalist H. G. Woodhead, analyzing foreign pressure as the primary catalyst for Japanese expansion in China. The author argues that Western colonial empires, having monopolized undeveloped territories, barred Japanese emigration, and raised discriminatory tariffs against Japanese manufactures, left Japan no alternative for economic survival but expansion onto the Asiatic mainland. Neville supplements the clippings with opinions from British Commercial Secretary H. A. Macrae, who contended that economic concessions would not satisfy Japan's drive for total regional hegemony, and E. Manico Gull of the China Association, who agreed that only substantial international trade outlets could divert Japanese advances.
subfiles.title: Urge Toward Expansion in Japan

subfiles.about: A document file note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 1450 concerning public reaction to the assassination of Major General Tetsuzan Nagata.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1450, dated August 23, 1935, filed under 894.20/145. The despatch examines the public reaction following the assassination of Major General Tetsuzan Nagata by a fellow officer. It notes that while the affair highlights the steep obstacles facing efforts to establish a disciplined army free from political intrigues, the murder itself was unlikely to carry broader political consequences.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Assassination of Major General Nagata

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo despatch No. 1532 regarding the appellate court ruling on civilian defendants in the May 15 Incident.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reviews Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 1532 regarding the judicial decisions rendered for civilian conspirators in the May 15, 1932 Incident. Turner reports that while seventeen defendants withdrew their appeals to receive an imperial amnesty celebrating the birth of the Crown Prince, the sentences of the remaining three were substantially reduced by the Court of Cassation. He underscores the unusual legal ruling that sentenced civilian participants under the Naval Criminal Code as accessories to naval officers.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1532 Regarding the May 15 Incident Trial

subfiles.about: Chargé Neville reports on the Court of Cassation's decision reducing sentences for civilian plotters of the May 15 Incident under the Naval Criminal Code.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1532 reports on the October 14, 1935 ruling by the Court of Cassation regarding the appeals of three civilian participants in the May 15, 1932 Incident: Dr. Shumei Okawa, Hidezo Toyama, and Kenichiro Homma. The high court materially reduced their sentences down to three to five years imprisonment, citing time already spent in detention. Most significantly, the court established a major legal precedent by ruling that previous courts erred in applying the Civil Criminal Code, holding instead that the civilians were accessories to naval officers and must be sentenced under the Naval Criminal Code for plotting against the State. Neville notes that the public welcomed the reduced sentences to balance the lenient terms previously given to military cadets and naval officers, and reports that procurators have begun reviewing the files of seventeen other civilian conspirators who had previously withdrawn their appeals.
subfiles.title: Decision of the Court of Cassation in the Case of the Civilian Participants in the May 15 Incident

subfiles.about: A document file note cross-referencing Tokyo Report No. 1545 regarding an admonition sent to the U.S. President by the Dai Nippon Seisan-to.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet records Tokyo Embassy Report No. 1545, dated November 13, 1935, filed under 811b.01/272. It references a nationalist resolution addressed to the President of the United States by the Dai Nippon Seisan-to (Great Japan Productive Industry Party).
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Document Addressed to the President by the Dai Nippon Seisan-to

subfiles.about: Chargé Neville reports the delivery of a resolution from the right-wing Dai Nippon Seisan-to demanding immediate Philippine independence.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1545 recounts an incident on November 13, 1935, when a delegation from the right-wing Dai Nippon Seisan-to (Great Japan Productive Industry Party) arrived at the American Embassy in Tokyo seeking to deliver a message directly to the President of the United States. Embassy officials refused to accept the document, explaining that communications must proceed through regular diplomatic channels via the Japanese Embassy in Washington, but the delegation left the resolution behind and cabled it directly to Washington. The enclosed translation, entitled 'An Admonition,' accuses the United States of granting an incomplete independence that contradicts historical pledges, asserting that the Japanese people are determined to oppose unlawful American actions in the Philippines in the interest of Far Eastern peace.
subfiles.title: Nationalist Party Petition Regarding Philippine Independence (Despatch No. 1545)

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the resignation of Count Makino as Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal due to illness and the appointment of Viscount Saito.
keywords: Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 254 announces that Count Nobuaki Makino resigned as Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal on December 26, 1935, due to persistent ill health and was immediately replaced by former Prime Minister Viscount Makoto Saito. Grew reports that Makino's poor health was the genuine reason for the resignation. The appointment of the moderate Viscount Saito is viewed as reassurance that radical political factions are unlikely to gain influence over the imperial throne.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 254 from Tokyo Regarding Resignation of Count Makino and Appointment of Viscount Saito

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum noting the receipt of translations of Imperial Ordinances Nos. 118 and 119 establishing cabinet advisory bodies.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum records the receipt of Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 1572 transmitting English translations of Imperial Ordinances Nos. 118 and 119. These ordinances promulgated the official organization of the Cabinet Inquiry Council (Naikaku Shingi Kai) and the Cabinet Investigation Bureau (Naikaku Chosa Kyoku), which had been examined in earlier embassy despatches.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1572 Transmitting Ordinances for Advisory Bodies

subfiles.about: Chargé Neville transmits English translations of Imperial Ordinances Nos. 118 and 119 establishing the Cabinet Inquiry Council and Investigation Bureau.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1572 transmits official translations of Japanese Imperial Ordinances Nos. 118 and 119, promulgated on May 10, 1935, detailing the statutory frameworks of the Cabinet Inquiry Council (Naikaku Shingi Kai) and the Cabinet Investigation Bureau (Naikaku Chosa Kyoku). Ordinance No. 118 outlines the composition and operational rules of the Inquiry Council, which is attached to the Cabinet and presided over by the Prime Minister to investigate and deliberate major state policies. Ordinance No. 119 establishes the administrative staffing, expert committees, and procedural powers of the Cabinet Investigation Bureau, authorizing it to conduct technical research and demand data from any government ministry.
subfiles.title: Transmission of Translations of Imperial Ordinances No. 118 and No. 119

subfiles.about: A State Department cover memorandum submitting a digest of Ambassador Grew's report on political and economic conditions in Japan at the start of 1936.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum, prepared by Division Chief Stanley K. Hornbeck for Under Secretary William Phillips and Secretary of State Cordell Hull, serves as a cover note introducing a digest of an Embassy despatch from Tokyo. The attached report reviews the political and economic landscape of Japan at the opening of 1936.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Digesting Tokyo Despatch on Japanese Situation at Turn of the Year

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo despatch No. 1612 regarding multiple manifestations of Japanese nationalism in 1935.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum digests Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 1612 of December 24, 1935, which reviewed concrete expressions of rising nationalism in Japan throughout 1935. Key developments cited include the formal notice of abrogation of the Washington Naval Treaty, demands for naval parity, withdrawal from the League of Nations, implementation of the Amau doctrine, and support for the North China autonomy movement. The memorandum also details internal ideological measures, such as the triumph of the fundamentalist imperial theory over Professor Minobe's organ theory, government consolidation of news agencies into the Domei Tsushinsha, and proposed legislation to restrict foreign automotive and petroleum companies.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1612 Regarding Nationalistic Tendencies in Japan

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo despatch No. 1630 on Japan's economic outlook and military ambitions in North China and Mongolia for 1936.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum provides a comprehensive digest of Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 1630 regarding the outlook for Japan in 1936. It notes that while internal industrial prosperity continues, rising public debt and international tariffs against Japanese exports present serious economic hazards. Regarding continental policy, the memorandum explains that while Kwantung Army forces remain restricted north of the Great Wall, the military seeks strategic domination over North China, Chahar, and Suiyuan without direct military occupation in order to exploit raw materials and counter Soviet communism. It concludes that Japanese energies will be steadily directed toward consolidating economic and strategic control over North China and Mongolia.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1630 Regarding General Situation Facing Japan in 1936

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew surveys the intensification of nationalist policies, diplomatic assertions, and ideological controls in Japan during 1935.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1612 reviews the substantial increase in Japanese nationalism and self-sufficiency efforts during 1935. Major international actions include the abrogation of the Washington Naval Treaty, persistent demands for a common naval ceiling, formal withdrawal from the League of Nations, enforcement of the Amau statement, and the military-backed autonomy movement in North China. Domestically, the Embassy notes the triumph of orthodox imperial ideology over Professor Minobe's liberal constitutional theories, the creation of the government-controlled Domei Tsushinsha news agency, and the government's decision to enact legislation restricting foreign automobile manufacturers from expanding operations in Japan.
subfiles.title: Nationalistic Tendencies in Japan
